lesson.title: Memory Tricks with Real Science Behind Them: Mnemonic Devices
lesson.summary: Mnemonic devices are structured encoding techniques, acronyms, imagery systems, and rhymes among them, that impose artificial organization or meaning on hard-to-remember material.
lesson.body:
Some information simply does not come with built-in meaning or structure: the order of planets, the notes on a musical staff, the bones of the wrist. Mnemonic devices are techniques that solve this problem by imposing artificial organization, imagery, or meaning onto material that would otherwise be arbitrary, making it far easier to encode and, later, to pull back out of memory.

Several mnemonic formats show up repeatedly in classrooms and in memory research. Acronyms compress a list into a single memorable word, such as ROY G BIV for the colors of the visible spectrum. Acrostics do the same job with a sentence instead of a word, where the first letter of each word in the sentence cues an item in the list to be remembered. The method of loci, one of the oldest recorded memory techniques, asks a person to imagine walking through a familiar place, such as their childhood home, and mentally placing one item to be remembered in each distinct location along the route. The peg-word system works similarly but uses a fixed, rhyming set of number-word pairs, one is bun, two is shoe, as permanent mental hooks that new items can be attached to through vivid imagery. The keyword method, often used for learning foreign vocabulary, links a new word to a familiar word that sounds similar and then builds a mental image connecting that familiar word to the new word's meaning.

Imagine a student using the method of loci to remember a list of the first ten amendments to the Constitution before a government exam. She imagines walking through her house: at the front door she pictures a giant scroll blocking the entrance (freedom of speech and religion), in the living room she imagines a soldier cleaning a musket on the couch (the right to bear arms), in the kitchen she pictures a police officer refusing to search the pantry without a warrant, and so on through each room. During the exam, she mentally walks back through her house in order, and each location triggers the image, and the image triggers the amendment.

Mnemonic devices work precisely because they force the kind of processing that earlier encoding strategies identify as effective. Placing an item at a specific location, or linking it to a vivid image, is elaborative encoding: it connects new, arbitrary material to something already familiar and meaningful. The imagery involved recruits a second, visual code alongside the verbal one, the same dual-coding benefit described in the discussion of encoding strategies. And because each mnemonic structure, a route through a house, a rhyming peg, an acronym, provides a built-in retrieval path, these devices also supply organization, giving the memory system a clear cue to follow back to the original information.

Mnemonics are best suited to material that is genuinely arbitrary, such as ordered lists, terminology, or number sequences. They are far less useful for building the kind of flexible, conceptual understanding an exam question about, say, the causes of a historical event requires, because memorizing a list of triggers is not the same as understanding how those triggers interact. The most effective students tend to use mnemonic devices to lock in the arbitrary scaffolding of a topic while relying on elaborative, meaning-based strategies for everything that actually requires understanding.
